Let’s dive into Chapter 6—The Hidden Machinery: How Tax Policy and Regulation Fuel Finance’s Dominance.
You know, it’s tempting to think that the rise of finance is all about smart people chasing big opportunities, or companies trying to be efficient. But if you look just below the surface, there's a whole web of rules and hidden incentives quietly tilting the playing field.
Think about it: tax codes, regulatory loopholes, government policies—they haven’t just let finance thrive, they’ve actually encouraged it every step of the way.
Picture this. It’s late during tax season, and a mid-career accountant is hunched over her desk, paperwork stacked high. As she works, she starts to notice something odd: her biggest clients—private equity firms, hedge funds, giant corporations—seem to operate by a totally different set of rules. Their profits are protected by clever deductions, offshore accounts, and special tax rates. Meanwhile, the small business owners she’s known for years are just struggling to keep their doors open, paying a bigger share of their income in taxes.
Most people never even notice how this machinery works. Take the carried interest loophole, for example. It lets private equity managers pay lower tax rates on their earnings than most teachers or nurses. And corporate tax codes? They actually reward companies for borrowing money to buy back their own shares, instead of investing in new equipment or hiring more workers.
And what about regulations that are supposed to protect the public? They’re often watered down or sidestepped by swarms of lobbyists and lawyers working behind the scenes.
It becomes clear—these rules aren’t neutral at all. They nudge companies to favor financial tricks over real investment, and they reward those who are savvy enough to navigate the system. That’s how finance keeps growing more powerful—not just because of market forces, but because the whole system is set up to make it happen.
For a lot of people, it just feels unfair. Our accountant can’t help but notice how her wealthiest clients always find new ways to game the system, while the folks with the least get left behind. That promise of a level playing field? With each passing year, it feels less like reality and more like a myth.
